title: The Dreaming Brain Burns Energy Even as Its Fuel Supply Rises
summary:
Ever woken up after a vivid dream feeling completely drained? Scientists at Tohoku University in Japan may have found the reason — and it's a paradox.

REM sleep, the stage linked to dreaming and memory processing, is often called "paradoxical sleep" because the body is mostly still while brain activity looks a lot like wakefulness. Now researchers have identified another paradox inside it. During REM sleep, the apparent energy supply to the brain increases — yet levels of ATP, the energy molecule neurons directly use, actually decline. The findings were published in Communications Biology.

"Ever felt exhausted after a vivid dream?" asks Professor Ko Matsui of Tohoku University. "Sleep may appear peaceful, but the brain is highly active — especially when dreaming. We were intrigued by this paradox, and wanted to look into the scientific basis behind why dreaming is somehow tiring."

To watch the sleeping brain in real time, the team used a UV-curable resin to make the skulls of mice transparent. Then they tracked brain blood volume as a sign of incoming fuel, along with neuronal ATP and astrocytic pyruvate, a compound that links glucose from the blood to energy metabolism in the brain.

During non-REM sleep, the researchers noticed small theta-band fluctuations in neuronal activity. These changes could predict shifts in brain blood volume several seconds later, suggesting the sleeping brain adjusts its blood vessels to match demand.

As the brain moved from non-REM into REM sleep, blood volume started to rise about 50 seconds before REM officially began — starting in the posterior cortex and moving forward. That suggests the brain prepares metabolically for REM sleep in advance. Once REM sleep began, pyruvate rose too. But neuronal ATP fell.

Why? Neurons may be using large amounts of ATP to reorganize memories, communicate between the hippocampus and cortex, or shift between brain circuits. Another possibility is that metabolic resources move differently from astrocytes to neurons during REM sleep. Whatever the mechanism, the dreaming brain seems to operate under unusually high energy demands — even while its fuel supply increases. So next time a dream leaves you wiped out, you'll know: your brain was working hard.
why_it_matters: Sleep is when the brain consolidates memories and clears out waste, so understanding why REM sleep is so metabolically expensive could eventually shape advice about sleep, studying and brain health — and it shows that even a 'resting' brain can be doing intense biological work.

questions.question: What paradox did the Tohoku University researchers identify during REM sleep?
options: The brain's apparent energy supply rises while ATP levels fall
Blood volume falls while neuron activity stops
The body moves more while the brain stays silent
The brain stops using energy while dreams become longer
questions.correct_answer: The brain's apparent energy supply rises while ATP levels fall

background_read: REM sleep was identified in the 1950s by researchers Eugene Aserinsky and Nathaniel Kleitman, who noticed that sleeping people's eyes dart rapidly back and forth during certain parts of the night.
A night's sleep moves through repeating cycles of light sleep, deep sleep and REM, each cycle lasting roughly 90 minutes — which is why most people dream several times before morning.
The human brain is only about 2% of body weight but consumes roughly 20% of the body's energy, and glucose delivered by the blood is its main fuel.

The hippocampus (a seahorse-shaped structure deep in the brain) and the cortex (the brain's wrinkled outer layer) work together to turn short-term experiences into lasting memories, a process that seems to happen largely during sleep.
The study was run by Tohoku University (a major research university in Sendai, Japan) and published in Communications Biology, a peer-reviewed science journal.

perspectives.perspective: Positive — a real step forward in sleep science
perspectives.description: For the first time researchers could watch fuel supply and energy use in the sleeping brain at the same time, in real time. That kind of window is rare, and it turns a familiar everyday feeling — waking up exhausted after a dream — into a measurable biological puzzle.

perspectives.perspective: Critical — mouse brains are not human brains
perspectives.description: The evidence comes from mice with surgically cleared skulls studied in a laboratory, so the exact numbers and timing may not transfer to people. The study also offers several possible explanations for falling ATP rather than settling on one, meaning the central mechanism is still unproven.

perspectives.perspective: Neutral — an old puzzle, a new angle
perspectives.description: Scientists have known since the 1950s that REM sleep looks oddly like wakefulness, and the brain's high energy appetite has been studied for decades. This work adds a metabolic dimension to a debate that has mainly been about brain electrical activity and dreaming.

perspectives.perspective: Forward-looking — where the research could go
perspectives.description: If REM's cost is tied to memory reorganization, future studies could test whether poor REM sleep damages learning or memory in students and older adults. Better understanding of astrocyte-to-neuron fuel transfer might also matter for conditions where brain energy supply fails.
